Content:
The most general way of solving exponential equations with different bases is to use logarithms on both sides of the equation.
For example, given the equation

Content:
[MATH: 3^{x+1} = 5^{x},]

Content:
we could apply [MATH: \log_3] on both sides and get

Content:
[MATH: \log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).]

Content:
Now, we use the fact that [MATH: \log_b \left( b^c \right) = c] to simplify the left-hand side:

Content:
[MATH: x + 1|= \log_{3} (5^{x})]

Content:
Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

Content:
[MATH: x + 1|= x\log_{3} (5)]

Content:
Finally, we solve for [MATH: x,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x + 1|= x\log_{3} (5); x − x\log_{3} (5)|= − 1; x(1 − \log_{3} (5))|= − 1; x|= − (1)/(1 − \log_{3} (5)); x|= (1)/(\log_{3} (5) − 1)]

Content:
Note: in the first step, we also could have applied [MATH: \log_5] on both sides of our equation, instead of [MATH: \log_3.] Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using [MATH: \log_5] instead of [MATH: \log_3.]
